rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology <U+2013> case study with semi-structured interviews (19 farmers, WUA presidents/secretaries, CHJ officials, technicians), policy document analysis and field observations; Figure 2 compiled from regional crop statistics 1983-2014. Q2: Transformations 1-3 and Discussion <U+2013> 1371 ha of former rain-fed slopes (38.9% of irrigated area) converted to drip, shift to citrus monoculture with higher crop water requirements, 88.2% of irrigated area now on groundwater, groundwater tables lowered and wells dried in La Font de la Figuera; authors conclude drip plus expansion and intensification led to more water use at watershed level. Q3: expansion shown both by official statistics (Figure 2, Table 1) and by stakeholder interviews (WUA president in Montesa explaining expansion uphill after well permit; technician and ex-president reporting dry wells). Q4: the mechanism (expanded irrigated area and crop shift) is quantified <U+2013> Table 1 crop areas by municipality, 1371 ha expansion, citrus 76% of Montesa irrigated produce, IVIA requirements 4114 m3/ha citrus vs 2053 vineyard. Q6: effect reported for the whole watershed (four municipalities, ~3500 ha irrigated). Q7: Transformation 2 <U+2013> expansion largest in Montesa and Vallada because they possess sufficient water, while in La Font de la Figuera lack of access to water hampered further expansion; expansion depended on well concessions from CHJ conditional on installing drip. Q8: Transformations section and Conclusions <U+2013> transformations cannot be solely attributed to drip irrigation as they relate to broader changes in Spanish agriculture and society.
rows.notes: Increased consumptive water use is inferred from area expansion, crop shift and crop water requirement figures (IVIA, Allen et al.) plus interview reports of falling groundwater; no direct measurement of water consumption or ET. Qualitative case study, no dispersion statistics.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology <U+2013> own interviews, document analysis and field observations in the C<U+00E0>nyoles watershed. Q2: Transformation 5 <U+2013> canals used before the shift to drip have been abandoned or disused, only one ancient weir (Montesa) remains operational, mills, pools and underground canals abandoned; WUA secretaries/presidents and farmers report unmaintained weirs, destroyed canals, non-preserved heritage. Q4: the intermediate step (replacement of surface irrigation infrastructure by wells) is quantified <U+2013> 3110 ha (88.2%) now irrigated from groundwater, surface irrigation only 413 ha (11.7%); lack of maintenance explained by farmers unable to cope with costs and administration giving no priority. Q6: reported across the four municipalities of the watershed. Q7: Transformation 5 <U+2013> demise of heritage results from public administration's non-conservation attitude and farmers being unable to cover maintenance costs, i.e. loss occurs where no institutional support for maintenance exists. Q8: Transformations section and Conclusions <U+2013> transformations cannot be attributed solely to drip; authors note ancient canals have been maintained elsewhere in Spain, implying site-specific outcome.
rows.notes: Evidence rests mainly on interview quotes; field observations are listed in the methodology but the heritage section does not clearly separate the authors' own observations from interviews and Pelejero (2013), so triangulation is doubtful. No quantification or dispersion measure of heritage loss.

notes: Qualitative socio-technical case study of one watershed (four municipalities) over 25 years; data from stakeholder interviews, official crop statistics and policy documents. No experimental or measured water-balance data.
